A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DDSBM research. Their text, equations, tables, figures and full appendices are accessible and support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between sections.

before.justification: v1 reports original ZINC250K and Polymer experiments, initial-coupling comparisons and graph-matching evaluations.

after.justification: v2 retains molecular experiments and reports additional graph-matching ablations, unconditional generation results on Community-20, Planar and QM9, and sampling-step sensitivity.

M1.justification: The CTMC reference process, alternating forward/backward IMF training, losses, graph-transformer parameterization and graph-matching procedure are retained. Algorithm 1 documents the existing procedure; the new derivation and ablation variants do not establish a change to the proposed method.

E1.justification: v2 adds unconditional generation on Community-20, Planar and QM9 in Appendix G. This substantially extends coverage from molecular property transformation to generation from a prior, including synthetic non-molecular graphs. ZINC250K and Polymer transformation remain.

E2.justification: The molecular comparators remain AtomG2G, HierG2G and DBM. New unconditional comparisons in Tables 10–12 add DiGress, ConGress, GraphRNN, GRAN, GG-GAN, SPECTRE, GraphAF, MoFlow, GraphDF, GDSS, GraphArm and GLAD. Most added baseline scores are explicitly taken from cited sources, rather than reported as new baseline training.

E3.justification: The molecular evaluation adds uniqueness, novelty and NSPDK. New unconditional experiments introduce DiGress-based splits, task-specific diffusion steps and training budgets, graph-feature MMD metrics and matched DBM/DDSBM epochs. Graph-matching controls and the QM9 sampling-step sweep further expand evaluation procedures; existing molecular splits and budgets are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained solver-quality and initial-coupling studies, v2 tests how matching algorithms affect final DDSBM performance and compares training with and without matching (Table 7, Figures 11–12). It also adds QM9 sampling-step sensitivity and generation trajectories, directly examining convergence, inference robustness and structural preservation.

E5.justification: v1's main results lack training-run counts and uncertainty estimates. v2 first reports three independently seeded training runs and supplies means and standard deviations in Tables 5–6. Appendix G additionally reports averaging five sampling repetitions. The PDFs do not establish an increase from a known earlier training-run count.

E6.justification: Existing values change: Table 1's DDSBM NLL moves from 162.228 to 160.461 and FCD from 0.896 to 0.833, now reported as three-run means. In the retained Tanimoto comparison, AtomG2G NLL changes from 346.499 to 289.674. New metrics, matching ablations, unconditional benchmarks and sampling-step results substantially expand reported outcomes.

T1.justification: The convergence theorem and most proofs are retained. Proposition A.6/B.6 corrects the normalization from mu_t(y) to mu_t(x) in the generator row-sum proof. v2 Section 4.2 also adds an explicit derivation connecting graph-vector transitions to permutation-invariant graph transitions, extending v1's verbal explanation.

C1.justification: The abstract's scientific claims, introduction contributions and concluding claims retain the same scope: discrete IMF with convergence, the graph-edit-distance connection and molecular optimization with limited structural changes. The added unconditional experiments do not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 interprets graph matching as accelerating convergence while being unnecessary for eventual convergence, and removes v1's concluding warning about its limitations for general graph tasks. It also adds explanations for reduced-step robustness, discusses the diversity advantage over latent models, and identifies QM9 validity/FCD versus novelty tradeoffs.

D1.justification: The existing molecular architecture, hardware, preprocessing and training budgets remain. v2 supplements them with algorithm pseudocode, a DDSBM code-access link, Pygmtools identification, explicit ZINC training/test counts of 23,936/5,984 pairs, and unconditional-generation hyperparameters. The newly disclosed sample counts do not establish a changed dataset split.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion largely retains its positioning. v2 acknowledges prior finite-state SB work through Chow et al. and explicitly distinguishes inherited IMF concepts from its discrete theoretical extension. It adds supporting references for NSPDK, Hungarian matching, Pygmtools, optimal transport exposition and GLAD.

P1.justification: Related work moves before theoretical background, which is substantially rewritten and expanded with a dedicated CTMC subsection. A new tutorial appendix explains SB and IMF through examples. The initial-coupling study moves into the appendices, and implementation, proofs and supplementary results are reorganized.

P2.justification: v2 expands the main tables with additional metric columns and adds uncertainty, ablation and generation tables. It introduces extensive explanatory schematics, convergence plots, generation trajectories and an NFE figure. Existing molecular examples and density plots are relocated, while the initial-coupling plot is redrawn.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical scrutiny: three-run uncertainty replaces unsupported precision, diversity metrics expose tradeoffs, and direct matching ablations test a central implementation choice. Broader generation and sampling-step evaluations, clearer exposition and additional reproducibility information improve assessment of the retained claims. Reporting imperfections remain, including conflicting NFE lists in Section G.5 and Figure 22's caption, but these are limited relative to the gains in validation.
